title: Snake and Ladder
brief: Design the classic board game. Players start off the board and take turns rolling a die. A ladder lifts a token up, a snake drops it down, and the first player to land exactly on the last square wins. Tests must be able to say exactly which numbers come up.

functional: A board of N squares with snakes and ladders, each a head square and a tail square.
Two or more players start off the board (position 0) and move in a fixed turn order.
A turn rolls the dice and moves the token by that many squares.
Landing on a snake head or ladder bottom moves the token to the tail, once.
A roll that would go past the last square is ignored: the token stays and the turn passes.
Landing exactly on the last square wins, and a finished game takes no more turns.
The dice is a swappable object, so a test can script the rolls.

idea.sentence: The board is just a lookup table from head to tail, and the only random thing in the game, the dice, sits behind an interface you can script.

jargon.plain: The game receives its dice from outside instead of creating it, so a test can hand in a fake one.
A stand-in object used in a test. Here a ScriptedDice returns numbers from a list you wrote.

patterns.name: Dependency injection
patterns.where: Game receives a Dice in its constructor.
patterns.why: No hidden Math.random. A test passes ScriptedDice and every game is replayable, so a win or an overshoot can be asserted exactly.

patterns.name: Data over code
patterns.where: Board keeps every snake and ladder as one map entry.
patterns.why: A snake and a ladder are the same thing, a jump. One lookup replaces two classes and a pile of if statements, and a new board is only new data.

decisions.question: Snake and Ladder as two classes?
decisions.choice: One jumps map, head to tail
decisions.because: Both do the same thing: move the token. The direction (tail below or above head) is data, so the game needs no type check.
decisions.instead: A Snake class and a Ladder class behind a Jump interface, with nothing different between them.

decisions.question: What if the roll goes past the last square?
decisions.choice: Ignore the move. The token stays and the turn passes. Only an exact landing wins.
decisions.because: It is the rule most families play and it gives every game a real ending to test. A different house rule is a different line in play(), not a different design.
decisions.instead: Bounce back from the end, or win on any roll that reaches the end.

decisions.question: Can a jump lead to another jump?
decisions.choice: No. The token jumps once and stays on the tail, even if the tail is another head.
decisions.because: Chains make the result depend on the table, and a loop (a snake whose tail is a ladder that goes back to the snake) would never end. One jump per landing is simple and always terminates.
decisions.instead: Follow jumps until a plain square, with cycle detection added to the board.

decisions.question: Where does the randomness live?
decisions.choice: Behind a Dice interface, injected into Game
decisions.because: Random code cannot be asserted. A scripted dice makes the whole game deterministic.
decisions.instead: Calling Math.random() or rand.Intn inside play().

followups.ask: Add an extra turn when a player rolls a six.
followups.answer: Change one line in play(): when the roll is 6 and the player did not win, do not advance the turn index. To keep the rule swappable, hand Game a small TurnRule interface that says whether this roll earns another turn. The board and the dice do not change.

followups.ask: Use two dice, or a loaded dice for a test.
followups.answer: Write another Dice. TwoDice rolls twice and adds. Game only calls roll(), so nothing else changes. A loaded dice is just ScriptedDice with a short list.

followups.ask: How do you stop a bad board, like a snake on the last square or a tail off the board?
followups.answer: Validate once, in a board constructor or factory: every head and tail must be between 1 and size, no head sits on the last square, and no head equals its own tail. Settle already ignores a head on the last square, but a clear error at setup is better than a silent rule.

followups.ask: Players join from different phones at the same time.
followups.answer: play() reads the turn, rolls and writes the position, so two calls could both move the same player. Put the game behind one lock, or a single goroutine or event loop that owns it and takes moves from a queue. Also check that the caller is the player whose turn it is.

watch.inputHint: Two arguments: the operation names, then each one's arguments. Game takes: size, [head, tail] pairs, number of players, scripted rolls. Example: ["Game","play"], [[10,[[3,7]],2,[3,1]],[]]

presets.label: A full game to the win

stages.title: Build the game
stages.note: The game owns the board and the players and is handed its dice. It never rolls anything itself.

stages.title: Roll
stages.note: The player whose turn it is asks the dice. The target square is the current square plus the roll.

stages.title: Move and settle
stages.note: If the target is on the board, ask the board to settle it: a snake or ladder moves the token once. If it is past the end, nothing moves.

stages.title: Win or pass the turn
stages.note: Standing on the last square wins and ends the game. Otherwise the turn passes to the next player.

gotchas.text: Decide and write down three rules: exact landing or not, what a jump landing on another jump does, and whether a six rolls again. Most Snake and Ladder bugs are one of these left unsaid.
Start at 0, off the board. Then the first roll is the same code as every other roll, and a snake back to the start is just a jump to 0.
Map.get returns undefined for a miss. Give a default with ?? (jumps.get(s) ?? s), and never test the result with a truthiness check such as ||, because a tail of 0 is falsy.
A map read of a missing key gives the zero value 0, which here is also a valid tail (the start). Use the two-value form (tail, ok := jumps[s]) to tell a miss from a jump to 0.
Keep players as []*Player. With []Player, for _, p := range players hands you a copy, and p.Pos = 5 changes the copy, not the player.

recap.key: The board is a head-to-tail map and the dice is an interface, so the game is a short loop you can replay exactly.
moves: Write the rules down first: exact landing, one jump, no extra turn
Model snakes and ladders as one map of jumps
Put the dice behind an interface and inject it
In play(): roll, settle if on the board, then win or pass the turn
